terms.grammar: adjective and noun, third declension; comparative senior
terms.comment: Of an old person, man or woman, and as a noun an old man (see old man); an old woman is anus (see old woman). “Get old” is senēscere.
Polite and a little formal, like “elderly”. Grandis alone is “big, full-grown” (see big).

terms.gloss: oldish; a little old man or woman
evidence: Cato Agr. 2.7: bovēs vetulōs (Lewis & Short, s.v. senex)
terms.comment: The diminutive of vetus, affectionate or slighting.

terms.register: Lewis & Short: a favourite word of the Augustan poets and of post-Augustan prose

phrases.latin: nec vērō dubitat agricola, quamvīs sit senex, quaerentī cui serat respondēre: ‘dīs immortālibus’
phrases.english: nor does the farmer, however old he is, hesitate to answer one who asks whom he is planting for: ‘for the immortal gods’

phrases.latin: cōnsurrēxisse omnēs illī dīcuntur et senem sessum recēpisse
phrases.english: they all stood up, it is said, and made room for the old man to sit
